title: Nero's fire
hookLine: Christians were blamed for the fire of Rome and killed as entertainment

lines: A HISTORIAN WHO DIDN'T LIKE THEM.
cards: The man who tells this story didn't like Christians. Tacitus was a Roman senator and historian, and he called their faith a harmful superstition. Yet his history of the emperors is where their story survives.
A fire broke out in Rome and raged through the city, burning whole districts. Afterward a rumor would not die: that the emperor Nero had wanted the fire. Relief for the homeless didn't stop it.
Prayers to the gods didn't stop it. Nero needed somebody else to blame.

teach.b: In his Annals, Tacitus says what happened next. To get rid of the rumor, Nero fastened the guilt on a group the crowd already hated, people called Christians.
Tacitus even explains the name: it came from Christus, executed under Tiberius by the governor Pontius Pilate. First, the arrests. Those who confessed were taken first.
Then, on what they disclosed, a great crowd of others, convicted, Tacitus says, not so much of setting the fire as of hatred of the human race.
Second, the killing was a show. Some were dressed in animal skins and torn apart by dogs. Some were nailed to crosses.
Some were set alight to serve as torches when daylight was gone. Nero opened his own gardens for it and mingled with the crowd.
Third, a turn from the man who disliked them. Tacitus still calls them guilty, deserving the harshest punishment.
Yet he writes that pity rose for them, because they were destroyed not for the public good, but to feed one man's cruelty. Fourth, what the Church remembers.
Nobody knows these martyrs' names. The Catholic calendar keeps a memorial for them anyway, the first martyrs of the Church of Rome, placed beside the feast of Peter and Paul.
Their story echoes a line from the First Letter of Peter, in the Douay-Rheims: "But if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name." Scapegoating didn't end in Rome.

When a city is afraid, a crowd still looks for someone to carry the fear: a minority, a newcomer, a neighbor who is different. Remembering these Christians makes it easier to see when it happens to anyone.

how: The Catholic calendar keeps a memorial for the first martyrs of the Church of Rome, killed under Nero, and Catholics often pray for persecuted people at Mass in the prayers of the faithful.

games.q: you're Nero. Rome has burned. relief and prayers to the gods haven't stopped the rumor that you wanted the fire. what do you do?
o: admit the rumor and step down.
find a hated group to blame.
ignore it and wait for it to pass.
games.why: Tacitus says Nero fastened the guilt on Christians. Tacitus, who thought them guilty all the same, says people came to pity them.

practice: Bring to mind someone blamed for what they didn't do: a group in the news, a kid at school, a coworker talked about when he leaves the room, maybe someone you've blamed yourself.
Don't argue the case; let them stand in your mind as a person, not a target. If you pray, pray for them and for the people doing the blaming.

wordCard.voice: Nero's fire. The burning of Rome, and the Christians the emperor blamed for it and killed as a public show. Today's word.
